title: Catholic Computer — starting principles
note: Each principle states a working commitment: something this initiative can be checked against, not only an aspiration.

principles.name: Privacy and ownership
principles.statement: Keep sensitive information under the user's control. Favor local processing, data minimization, inspectable data flows, and the ability to export or delete what a system holds.

principles.name: Free will and conscience
principles.statement: No covert persuasion, engineered dependency, or exploitation of personal vulnerabilities. People must remain free to question, disagree, decide, and disconnect.

principles.name: Decentralized intelligence
principles.statement: Explore open models, portable agents, interoperable tools, and computing infrastructure that individuals and communities can run or choose for themselves.

principles.name: Truth and accountability
principles.statement: Make claims traceable to sources and technical results reproducible. Be clear about uncertainty. Keep people responsible for consequential decisions.

principles.name: Subsidiarity and the common good
principles.statement: Support the autonomy of families, parishes, schools, and local communities. Share knowledge and tools so advanced computing is useful beyond large institutions.

principles.name: Stewardship
principles.statement: Use compute responsibly. Favor efficient models, durable hardware, repairability, and transparent resource costs when choosing how to build.

signatures.description: People who have added their name in personal support of these principles. Clergy and religious sign as individuals; a signature implies nothing about a diocese, order, parish, or the Holy See.
